title: Air India Crew Member's Missed Ganpati Puja Found Her at 35,000 Feet
excerpt: Anuradha Soni thought her flight roster had cost her the family's Ganpati Puja. Then a passenger boarded with a Ganesha idol — and the celebration came to her.
body:
• Anuradha Soni, an Air India cabin crew member, missed her family's Ganpati Puja at home after her flight roster was changed.
  • During a later flight, a passenger unexpectedly boarded with a Ganpati idol — right at the time of the festival.
  • Anuradha performed a small puja inside the aircraft and shared the emotional video on Instagram, where it went viral.

Anuradha Soni was supposed to be home for Ganpati Puja this year. Instead, she was working an Air India flight — her roster changed at the last minute, and the family celebration she had planned around went ahead without her. Somewhere between the meal service and the seatbelt checks, she thought to herself, "Bappa, is baar aapki puja miss ho jaegi" — this year, I will have to miss your puja.

Bappa, it turned out, had other plans.

On another flight shortly after, a passenger walked down the aisle carrying something Anuradha never expected to see at 35,000 feet: a Ganpati idol, brought along for the very festival she was missing. She welcomed the passenger and the idol, and performed a small puja right inside the aircraft — a prayer that had been denied her at home, completed in the galley of a commercial jetliner.

"Sometimes, Bappa has a way of making you feel His presence exactly when you need it the most. There I was… at 35,000 feet… doing my puja, saying my prayers, and taking Bappa's blessings. At that moment, it genuinely felt like Bappa was telling me… Main tumhare saath hoon, chahe tum kahin bhi ho."

— Anuradha Soni, writing on Instagram (@fromcrewtocrayons)

Anuradha posted the video to her Instagram account, where it quickly spread. Commenters called it "so lucky and such a sweet gesture," while another wrote that "when your devotion, love, faith and belief are true from inside… Pritam always finds a path towards his devotee." A third wished aloud to have been on the same flight: "Wow, I wish I was there on the same flight with you, Ma'am."

Festivals and the people who work through them

For cabin crew, pilots, nurses, doctors, and countless others on shift rosters, missing a festival is an ordinary fact of working life. Ganesh Chaturthi is one of India's most home-centered celebrations — the idol is welcomed into the house, the family gathers, the aarti is sung together. Missing it stings in a way that goes beyond any one ritual; it is the sound of everyone you love celebrating without you.

That is why the story landed the way it did. Anuradha's caption carried a second line that thousands echoed back at her: "Jo hum plan karte hain, usse kahin zyaada achha Bappa ka plan hota hai" — Bappa's plan is always far better than the one we make ourselves. The sentiment is familiar to anyone who has ever been bumped off a holiday by a work schedule and then found the celebration showing up in an unexpected place.

A story the diaspora knows by heart

For Indians living abroad, the missed-festival feeling is a permanent condition rather than an occasional one. NRIs routinely celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi thousands of miles from their families — often on a different weekend, often on a video call, often alone in an apartment while the family group chat fills with photos of the idol at home.

There is something pointed about this particular festival finding Anuradha on an Air India flight. Air India is, for many in the diaspora, the bridge home — the airline on which they fly back for exactly these celebrations. That the puja she missed at home arrived mid-flight, carried aboard by a stranger, makes the story feel almost designed for the millions of Indians who worship from a distance.

Why it went viral

The video had every ingredient of a viral moment: genuine emotion, an unscripted surprise, and a payoff that arrived within seconds. But it also carried none of the cynicism that usually accompanies feel-good content online. Anuradha's tears were not performative — they were the tears of someone whose quiet resignation had just been overturned by a stranger's kindness.

Nor did anyone treat the puja itself as a novelty. The comments were devotional rather than amused, which is rarer than it sounds on an internet that loves to turn everything into a meme. The story stayed sweet because the moment was real: a crew member who thought she had lost the festival, finding it again at cruising altitude.
image_caption: Air India cabin crew member Anuradha Soni with the Ganpati idol carried aboard her flight. A passenger had brought the idol along, letting her perform the Ganpati Puja she had missed at home.
nri_angle: Air India is the diaspora's bridge home, and this story of a missed festival being found at 35,000 feet speaks directly to NRIs who routinely celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi thousands of miles from family.
author: Diaspora Desk
